title: The Meta Quest 3S is on sale for $297 — which is basically its old price
teaser: The Meta Quest 3S is on sale for $296.79, but users should know it uses older Fresnel lenses, lacking the superior optics of the pricier Quest 3.
summary:
The Meta Quest 3S VR headset is available for $296.79, representing a slight discount from its previous price. The standalone unit is a compromise product, sharing the Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 processor, color passthrough cameras, and controllers with the high-end Quest 3.
However, the 3S uses Fresnel lenses (like the older Quest 2), which limits its optical quality compared to the Quest 3. The Quest 3 remains superior due to its advanced pancake lenses, which offer higher image quality and resolution per eye. Despite these hardware limitations, the 3S offers a functional entry point into wireless VR gaming, playing titles like Batman: Arkham Shadow and supporting Steam streaming.
author: Antonio G. Di Benedetto
content: The Meta Quest 3S VR headset with 128GB of storage is $296.79 (about $53 off) at Amazon . This is Meta's entry-level VR headset, which launched back in 2024 for $299.99 before getting a price increase this year to $349.99 . So it's not exactly the most exciting deal, but it's about as good as you're likely to find these days for a new unit. The base model Quest blends a bit of the higher-end Quest 3 and older Quest 2 for a Goldilocks-style compromise. Like other Quests, it's a standalone unit that operates wirelessly - until it's time to charge it, of course. It plays a wide selection of games from the Quest store, like Batman: Arkham Shadow and Supernatural ( once it relaunches ), and if you don't mind some added latency, you can wirelessly stream Steam games from your PC. While the much pricier Quest 3 uses lighter, flatter pancake lenses for its optics, the 3S uses fresnel lenses just like the Quest 2 generation. But other than that, it's got many similarities as the $600 Quest 3: the same Qualcomm Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 processor, the same cameras with color passthrough video, and the same controllers. What you pay much more for in the Quest 3 is higher image quality, thanks in part to those refined optics and a higher resolution per eye. But the Quest 3S still looks fine with its 1832 x 1920 pixels per eye. It's a shame we're no longer seeing the previous kinds of low prices the Quest 3S used to fall to, like when it was $249 around Black Friday, but with the way things are going this is as good as it gets for now.

title: The Nex Playground is down to its pre-RAMageddon price during Prime Day
teaser: The Nex Playground is back on sale for $239 during Prime Day, but remember: consistent gameplay requires a paid subscription!
summary: During Prime Day, the family-friendly Nex Playground console is on sale for $239, marked down from its MSRP of $299. While the motion-based console is appealing to parents, players must note that consistent play requires a paid subscription, such as the 3-month Play Pass for $49. Beyond the Nex, major consoles like the Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S are also subject to discounts on physical and digital games. Consumers can save on accessories like controllers and headsets, though major discounts on PS5 SSDs are unlikely.
author: Allison Johnson
content: The Nex Playground is the family-centric, Kinect-like game console that made one Verge editor's kids laugh, cry, and ask for more playtime , even when they were sick. The motion-based game play isn't perfect, but it has won over plenty of parents - and it's on sale for $239 at Amazon , down from its current MSRP of $299. That's a healthy discount, though only slightly better than the Nex's original $250 price. Like so many other gadgets, the Nex Playground became a victim of RAMageddon when its price went up in April . It got a $60 discount shortly after for Amazon's week of gaming deals - and again with this Prime Day deal - but it's nothing like the $199 prices we saw before the RAM crisis hit. This is the new normal, I guess. Still, any discount is welcome, especially when you'll need a subscription if you want to play more than a few starter games. You can get a 3-month Play Pass for $49 to access a much deeper catalog of games, or pay $89 for a 12-month pass. The subscription economy and RAMageddon come for us all, but at least a sale can take a little bit of the sting out of it.

title: Digital indigestion: Fizzy Coca-Cola display chokes on full storage
teaser: Digital indigestion: A Coca-Cola display in the Azores flashed a 'storage full' error, hilariously exposing the internal workings of the digital signage.
summary: An unusual digital sign in the Azores, featuring a Coca-Cola display, was spotted exhibiting a 'storage full' error, humorously dubbed 'digital indigestion.' The warning was suspected to stem from the operating system, possibly Ubuntu, which flashed an alert that the storage volume was full. The piece notes that while such tech issues are common (like an over-caffeinated techie), modern digital signage is supposed to keep its internal workings hidden from the public. The article uses this instance to comment on the visible nature of technological failures.
content: offbeat Digital indigestion: Fizzy Coca-Cola display chokes on full storage Ubuntu warning bubbles up on an Azores advertising screen BORK!BORK!BORK! Are you a glass-half-full or glass-half-empty person? Some distressed digital signage on the island of São Miguel in Portugal's Azores is running on empty, judging by today's entry into the files of signage silage. Spotted by an eagle-eyed Register reader, a Coca-Cola display has clearly had too much of the carbonated beverage and urgently needs to free up some space, a feeling many an over-caffeinated techie will be familiar with after chugging one Diet Coke too many. Not quite the real thing Supplied It's tricky to work out what operating system is running behind the scenes. Running Windows with 200 MB or so of disk space is only for the brave (or foolhardy), but we suspect this might be Ubuntu Unity warning onlookers that the volume is fit to burst. While there is an option to ignore the message (assuming the viewer can find somewhere to plug in a mouse or keyboard), doing so might be the computing equivalent of dropping some Mentos into a bottle of Coke and standing well back. While a good old-fashioned poster would never show an error message, thus obscuring whatever message Coca-Cola is trying to convey via the medium of a bottle top, Ubuntu isn't a bad choice for digital signage. Assuming it is indeed the operating system running behind the scenes, security maintenance could continue well past the display's lifetime, and there are plenty of tools to deploy, provision, and manage the hardware. All of which makes the pop-up a little incongruous. Somewhere, a distant dashboard is flashing red to indicate the signage storage is not what it might be. But on a well-managed system, surely the customer would never be aware of any issues. Kiosks and digital signs are about keeping their internals well tucked away from prying eyes after all. Except here. A volume is getting dangerously full. The same effect can be created by pouring a sachet of Pop Rocks/Space Dust* into one's mouth and chugging a glass of Coke. The result could be your very own storage error. Possibly through your nostrils. ® *Also known as popping candy.

title: Xteink’s tiny e-readers are 20 percent off for Prime Day
teaser: Grab a pocket-sized e-reader! The Xteink X4 and X3 are 20% off for Prime Day, featuring magnetic mounts for your phone.
summary: Xteink is offering deep discounts on its miniature e-readers, the X4 and X3, during Prime Day. The X4 is now $55.20 (regularly $69), and the X3 is $63.20 (normally $79). These devices are praised for being smaller and more pocketable than Kindles and Kobos, and they include magnetic mounts that stick to MagSafe-compatible smartphones. While the bundled software can be basic, users can upgrade to the free CrossPoint Reader firmware. The X4 offers good battery life and multiple ways to load content, though it lacks a dedicated online bookstore. The smaller X3 features an improved button layout and excellent portability, though it relies on a proprietary magnetic USB charging cord.
author: Andrew Liszewski
content: The Xteink X4 and smaller X3 e-readers are discounted to $55.20 (regularly $69) and $63.20 (normally $79), respectively, as part of Amazon's Prime Day promotions this week. Both e-readers are significantly smaller and more pocketable than any of the Kindle and Kobo models currently available, and feature magnetic mounts so they can be stuck to the back of MagSafe-compatible smartphones. The bundled software is a little rough around the edges, but the versions Amazon is selling can both be easily upgraded to the free CrossPoint Reader firmware featuring a more polished user interface. In our hands-on with the X4 , we liked that the e-reader features several buttons that are used to turn the pages of an ebook, but struggled with navigating its sometimes challenging bundled software using buttons in lieu of a touchscreen. Battery life is excellent, and the e-reader provides several different ways to load up books and other documents, but keep in mind you won't have access to a dedicated online bookstore like Kindles and Kobos feature. The X3's functionality is similar to the X4, but with a smaller design, an improved button layout, and broader compatibility with smaller smartphones featuring magnetic mounts on the back. It's even easier to stash in a small pocket, but the X3's dependence on a proprietary magnetic USB charging cord could be a deal breaker for those prone to losing cables.
